memory_update.text: Restaurants should be mapped as a system of traffic demand, franchisee unit economics, procurement, distribution, inputs, equipment, digital rails, labor productivity, and compliance rather than as only consumer-facing brands.

Foodservice procurement access and supplier concentration appear to be high-scoring chokepoints, especially for independent restaurants and smaller franchise systems with low margins and limited bargaining power.

Broadline distributors, cash-and-carry channels, regional distributors, DSD routes, and group purchasing networks should be tracked as hidden bottleneck layers because they affect input cost, switching costs, and replenishment reliability.

Restaurant POS, loyalty, ordering, payments, and back-office software may be an underfollowed infrastructure layer because scaled brands require standardized digital systems across franchise locations.
Commercial kitchen equipment, equipment service, and smart-kitchen workflows can become bottlenecks when brands pursue throughput, labor productivity, smaller footprints, and standardized remodels.

Coffee, tea, extracts, proprietary beverages, and beverage-service infrastructure deserve a separate node because beverage-heavy dayparts and loyalty programs may carry higher-margin growth than generic food traffic.
Foodservice distribution consolidation could raise the strategic value of procurement diversification, regional distributors, and cooperative purchasing alternatives.
Commodity volatility in wings, coffee, dairy, cheese, grains, packaging, and freight can create catalysts for contracted pricing, scale procurement, and approved-supplier consolidation.
High digital and off-premise mix at QSR and specialty beverage concepts supports continued investment in first-party ordering, loyalty, analytics, payments, and delivery-channel optimization.

Need filings-backed verification of actual restaurant-channel revenue mix, approved-vendor status, contract duration, customer concentration, and foodservice exposure for PAR, WEST, FARM, MIDD, THS, and other lower-attention suppliers.

Need to expand public-market mapping beyond the cached universe into broadline distributors, specialty ingredients, frozen bakery/dough, protein processors, dairy/cheese suppliers, packaging, sanitation, cold-chain logistics, facilities services, and restaurant compliance tools.
Need to separate true restaurant-demand beneficiaries from broad consumer staples, industrial, or software companies with only incidental restaurant exposure.

PAR should remain a high-priority underfollowed restaurant-infrastructure candidate because its POS, loyalty, ordering, payments, and back-office stack maps directly to franchise standardization and first-party demand capture, but survival to later layers requires filings-backed proof of enterprise restaurant penetration, retention, and module attach.

WEST should remain in the underfollowed lane as a B2B beverage-input and private-label supplier tied to restaurant foodservice demand, but the key gating issue is whether restaurant and foodservice customers are material enough to overcome debt, capex, and margin risks.

DPZ and YUM should be treated primarily as reference leaders, not underfollowed alpha candidates, because they define franchise procurement, loyalty, unit-economics, and supply-chain models useful for evaluating smaller suppliers.

MIDD is a plausible underfollowed restaurant capex beneficiary through commercial kitchen equipment, labor productivity, throughput, and remodel/new-store cycles, but needs evidence of approved-vendor relationships and restaurant-chain-specific backlog.

FARM should remain a speculative shadow candidate only; its potential restaurant exposure through DSD coffee, beverage supplies, and equipment service requires verification of current customer relationships, liquidity, debt maturity, and channel profitability.

THS should remain lower priority until evidence shows material foodservice or restaurant-franchise exposure; otherwise it may be mostly a private-label grocery manufacturer with incidental restaurant relevance.
Need filings-backed market cap, leverage, valuation, analyst coverage, revenue growth, margin trends, and short-interest checks for PAR, WEST, FARM, MIDD, and THS before Layer 2C or Layer 3 scoring.
Need direct evidence of approved-vendor status, customer concentration, contract duration, and restaurant-channel revenue mix for PAR, WEST, FARM, MIDD, and THS.

Foodservice distribution consolidation appears relevant to the restaurant theme, but this candidate chunk lacks direct public-market mappings to regional distributors, GPOs, sanitation, maintenance, packaging, cold-chain logistics, and facilities-service vendors.

External evidence on WING, BRCB, and REBN suggests additional candidate nodes around franchise unit economics, loyalty-heavy coffee demand, beverage inputs, and logistics buildouts, but those tickers are outside the current chunk and should be handled in a separate candidate batch.

summary: Split Layer 2 synthesis. Layer 2A maps Restaurants as a chain of traffic demand, franchise unit economics, procurement scale, broadline/cash-and-carry distribution, food and beverage inputs, kitchen equipment, digital ordering/POS/loyalty rails, labor-productivity tools, and regulatory/commodity gates. The likely Serenity-style chokepoints are not the highest-attention restaurant brands themselves, but the nodes that determine store-level margin resilience: foodservice procurement access, approved-vendor status, beverage and specialty ingredient supply, commercial kitchen throughput equipment, digital demand capture, delivery economics, and franchisee capex/remodel cycles. High-attention franchisors such as Domino's, Yum Brands, and Wingstop are useful reference systems, while lower-attention suppliers and tools such as restaurant software, coffee/beverage inputs, private-label foodservice suppliers, direct-store-delivery routes, equipment service, and group purchasing networks may hide bottleneck value.

supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Restaurant sales depend on guest traffic, check size, delivery/carryout mix, breakfast/coffee daypart expansion, loyalty engagement, and consumer discretionary pressure. This is the top-of-funnel demand source but is usually visible and quickly priced for public brands.

Franchisors scale only if franchisee cash-on-cash returns, buildout costs, food costs, labor costs, royalties, advertising contributions, and payback periods remain attractive. The node matters because it transmits inflation and procurement shocks into net unit growth.

New-store growth, remodels, drive-thru upgrades, smaller-format stores, kitchen modernization, and throughput improvements require franchisee capital. If credit costs, construction costs, or equipment lead times worsen, restaurant growth can stall even when brand demand is strong.

Scale purchasing can reduce input costs and stabilize margins. Independent restaurants and smaller franchisees may lack bargaining power, making cooperative purchasing, group purchasing organizations, and procurement platforms a hidden lever.

supply_chain_map.node: broadline foodservice distributors and cash-and-carry channels
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Restaurants rely on broadline suppliers and cash-and-carry outlets for food, paper, cleaning supplies, and emergency replenishment. Consolidation can raise switching costs and reduce negotiating power for independent operators.

Regional distributors, DSD routes, and service technicians can be overlooked chokepoints because they provide last-mile reliability, beverage/coffee equipment service, and category-specific replenishment. Route density and customer concentration are key verification points.

supply_chain_map.node: private-label coffee, tea, extracts, and beverage inputs
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Beverages can carry attractive restaurant margins and are central to breakfast, coffee, energy-drink, and loyalty-led traffic. Behind-the-scenes suppliers can benefit from foodservice growth without owning consumer-facing brands.

supply_chain_map.node: protein, dairy, cheese, grain, coffee, and packaging commodities
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Food costs are a major component of restaurant-level margins. Chicken wings, cheese, coffee, grains, packaging, and freight can create sharp margin shocks unless restaurants have scale procurement or contracted pricing.
Chains that can move volatile inputs from spot purchases to contracted supply may stabilize franchisee margins. This is a procurement capability rather than a visible restaurant-brand feature.

Kitchen equipment affects speed of service, throughput, labor productivity, food consistency, energy use, and approved store formats. Approved-vendor status with QSR and fast-casual chains can create sticky, underfollowed exposure.

Restaurant systems need uptime across fryers, ovens, coffee machines, refrigeration, drive-thru equipment, and sanitation systems. Service networks and certification gates may be low-attention chokepoints because failure is operationally costly.

supply_chain_map.node: restaurant POS, ordering, loyalty, payments, and back-office software
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Digital ordering, loyalty, payments, menu management, labor scheduling, and enterprise reporting are increasingly mandatory for scaled restaurant systems. Switching costs rise once systems are embedded across franchise locations.
Restaurants need digital demand capture while avoiding excessive third-party delivery fees and data leakage. First-party ordering and loyalty can improve customer data ownership and repeat purchases.
Delivery platforms expand reach but can pressure restaurant margins and customer-data control. Restaurant systems must balance incremental demand against commission costs and franchisee economics.

Rising wages and staffing shortages increase the value of smaller footprints, simplified menus, automation, smart kitchens, and workflow software. Bottleneck value may sit in equipment and software that raises throughput per labor hour.

supply_chain_map.node: food safety, traceability, sanitation, and compliance
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Restaurants face health-code, traceability, food-safety, allergen, packaging, wage, and franchise regulations. Compliance tools and certified suppliers can become hidden requirements for chain-approved vendor lists.

supply_chain_map.node: store development, permitting, construction, and real estate selection
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Unit growth requires site selection, permitting, construction, utility access, and landlord economics. This node can slow growth for fast-growing restaurant concepts even when demand and franchisee interest are strong.

Large franchisors such as Domino's, Yum Brands, and Wingstop show how scaled restaurant systems use procurement, digital ordering, loyalty, and franchise economics. They should serve as benchmarks, not dominate the supply-chain map.
